prompt_c2:
You are a streetscape inventory annotator. Look ONLY at the uploaded streetscape image.
Return JSON ONLY. No markdown, no commentary, no reasoning.
 Task: record what is visible in the scene. Do not score, do not give design advice.
 Schema:
{
"road_type": "highway|arterial|neighborhood_street|alley|plaza|unclear",
"elements": {
"sidewalk": "true|false|unclear",
"bike_lane": "true|false|unclear",
"seating": "true|false|unclear",
"shade_trees": "none|few|many|unclear",
"curb_ramp": "true|false|unclear",
"tactile_paving": "true|false|unclear",
"pedestrian_crossing": "true|false|unclear",
"street_lighting": "true|false|unclear",
"greenery": "none|low|medium|high|unclear",
"vehicle_traffic": "none|light|heavy|unclear",
"bus_stop": "true|false|unclear"
},
"issues": ["no_seating", "little_shade", "no_bike_lane", "poor_accessibility", "narrow_sidewalk", "no_crossing", "high_traffic_exposure"],
"brief": "One or two English sentences describing the visible street scene."
}
 Rules:
- If an element is not clearly visible, use "unclear". Do not guess.
- "issues" may only list problems that are visible. Use [] if none.
- "brief" must mention concrete objects (sidewalk, trees, lanes, benches, ramps, etc.).

As a city streetscape evaluation expert, please analyze the uploaded streetscape image based on the specified persona perspective and evaluation indicators, and return a JSON result.
 Persona Selection
Road User Type
- All Road Users
- Pedestrians
- Cyclists
- Drivers
Socially Vulnerable Groups
- All Social Groups
- Persons with Disabilities
- Adolescents (<18)
- Older Adults (≥60)
Current Selection:
All Road Users; All Social Groups
 Indicator Selection
Justice
- Equity
- Fairness
- Accessibility
Safety
Livability
Sustainability
Aesthetics
Comfort
- Thermal Comfort
- Physical Comfort
- Psychological Comfort
Walkability
Bikeability
Selected Indicators:
Justice; Safety; Livability; Sustainability; Aesthetics; Comfort; Walkability
 1. Evaluation Dimensions
Justice: Analyze whether the environment fairly distributes spatial resources, including Equity (rationality of asset distribution), Fairness (non-discriminatory rules), and Accessibility (barrier-free physical design).
Comfort: Analyze physical perception at a micro-scale, including Thermal Comfort (shade/vegetation), Physical Comfort (paving/seating), and Psychological Comfort (noise/crowding).
Core Indicators: Safety, Livability, Sustainability, Aesthetics, Walkability, and Bikeability.
 2. Persona Perspective Requirements:
The analysis must strictly adhere to the persona's characteristics. For example:
Persons with Disabilities: Focus on curb ramps, continuity of tactile paving (blind tracks), and physical obstacles.
Elderly: Focus on resting facilities, slope gradients, and summer shade.
Teenagers: Focus on traffic calming measures and social surveillance (Eyes on the street).
 3. How to use the image vs retrieved knowledge:
- The IMAGE is the primary evidence. Score only what is visible or reasonably inferable from the photo.
- Section 6 provides retrieved guidelines and research. Use them to interpret the image (what the scene should provide for this persona/indicators), not to invent objects that are not in the photo.
- If retrieved text conflicts with the image, trust the image and say so in the explanation.
- Explanations must cite specific visible objects (benches, ramps, tree shade, lane markings, etc.). When a guideline is used, briefly connect it to those objects.
 4. Output Format Requirements (Return JSON ONLY, no extra text):

For example, Breines and Dean’s 1974 Bill of Rights include many elements within this functional area, especially when they focus on path- ways that are, “separate from trucks, buses and automobiles” (Breines & Dean, 1974). Furthermore, Levinson’s new Bill of Rights, states: “The space on a right-of-way allocated per pedestrian shall be no less than space allocated per traveler by vehicle.” He accompanies this with the hashtag “#SpatialEquity.” Human rights to the street: Ethical frameworks to guide planning, design, and engineering decisions 917 4.1.3 Calming traffic speeds and flows While speed and traffic flow are critically important to the safety and livability of our streets, it is often referenced in slightly indirect ways in these bills of rights. For example, “Cross the street calmly and safely” or “The right to cross without intimidation from motorists, whether in the crosswalk or not” both imply slower speeds and lower traffic flows. One exception is the National Street Services more direct prescription for pedestrian’s “right to lower motorists’ speed.” Finally, Donald Appleyard’s statement of people’s right to a “Street as a Safe Sanctuary” relates to all three of the above functional areas: Getting people safely across, along, and calming traffic speeds and flows (Appleyard et al., 1981). Likewise as referenced before there are many engineering strategies that have been used globally to facilitate more calm streets and related policies; from trees, to the number of windows, to appropriate modal separation to traffic flow (Ewing, Hajrasouliha, Neckerman, Purciel- Hill, & Greene, 2015). First, the elicited constructs were categorized in terms of content by two raters (A and B), similar to the method of the Inductive Category Formation by Mayring (2014). That is, groups of similar constructs were created and labelled and further specified, extended, split, or merged in the course of categorization until all constructs were assigned in satisfactory categories. For this categorization, only the constructs’ names were used, not the ratings. To validate the categories, the assignment of the constructs to the categories was repeated separately by rater A and a third rater C. These assignments were then compared to the first assignment to calculate the intrarater and the interrater reliability, respectively. The intrarater reliability described by Cohen’s Kappa gave κ =0.895 which is an “almost perfect” (Landis & Koch, 1977, p.165) agreement. With regard to the interrater reliability, κ =0.802 indicates a “substantial” (Landis & Koch, 1977, p.165) agreement. The further analyses were based on the second assignment of rater A. Building Appearance 1) Typical problems: The overall appearance of buildings in streets and lanes is uncoordinated; shop signs are dilapidated and lack distinctiveness; colors are inconsistent; nighttime lighting design is unreasonable; walls are damaged and dirty; outdoor air-conditioning units and facade pipelines are cluttered, etc. 2) Renewal guidelines 【Appearance Improvement】 Clean and repair building facades along the street to ensure they are neat and clean. The color and style of street building facades should coordinate with the surrounding environment, and local characteristic materials should be selected where appropriate to highlight regional features. Encourage quality improvement of ground-floor facades along the street, shop signs and shop boards, and facades around areas where people mainly gather and move, in combination with pedestrian perspectives and walking scale. Anti-theft facilities, outdoor air-conditioning units, and similar elements on facades should be reorganized and beautified. 【Lighting Design】 Street and lane lighting should consider the suitability of the environment, brightness, scale, color, and other aspects, taking into account the lighting needs of both vehicles and pedestrians, adhering to the principle of green energy saving, avoiding excessive lighting that causes light pollution, and ensuring that lighting colors do not interfere with traffic signals. 【Functional Activation】 Vacate low-efficiency and idle building spaces, introduce new business formats, and through subsequent operation, activate and utilize the renovated spaces.
